rationale: A wins because it has discipline where B grabs the hot wire. A refuses "Klarna won't say how many jobs the AI cut" as "not an angle you pitch," which is exactly the adult move; B leads with "It won't say how many people lost their jobs," turning ambiguity into a loaded allegation. B has usable shapes, but its consumer line "a chatbot may be the first one to rule on it" spends proof it does not have.
gaps_in_A: "The machine takes the two-thirds that were resolvable in minutes" is an inference, not a supplied fact. The update says the assistant handles two-thirds of chats, not that those were the easy tickets.
"Klarna's AI does the work of 700 agents" makes the 700-agent number sound current and ongoing; the update says it handled that equivalent work "in its first months."
"24hr" decay on the IPO economics angle is too tight. A pending public filing keeps cost-structure scrutiny alive longer than a same-cycle markets hit.
"When the chatbot handles the dispute" still leans on an unproven premise. The update says advocates raised concerns about AI handling disputes, not that Klarna's assistant actually decides them.
gaps_in_B: "It won't say how many people lost their jobs" overstates the fact pattern. The update says Klarna will not split roles cut from roles left unfilled, and that headcount fell partly through attrition.
"a chatbot may be the first one to rule on it" is not grounded. Handling disputes is not the same as ruling on disputes, and the update does not prove either for Klarna's assistant.
"AI-shrunk cost base" asserts the cost base shrank because of AI. The update gives headcount, profitability, and automation numbers, not support-cost or opex proof.
"The update is fresh" is placeholder timeliness. A real why-now names the disclosure, filing stage, regulator action, or dated advocate pressure.
